sections.content: George Orwell was the pen name of Eric Arthur Blair, born on 25 June 1903 in Motihari in the Bengal Presidency of British India, now in Bihar, India. His father worked in the Opium Department of the Indian Civil Service. A year after his birth, his mother took Eric and his siblings to England, where he grew up and later won a scholarship to Eton College. After leaving Eton in the early 1920s, he did not have the funds to continue to university, so he joined the Indian Imperial Police in Burma and served there for about five years. The experience gave him a painful close-up view of colonial exploitation and deeply shaped his later politics. In 1927, after falling ill, he returned to Europe and decided to become a writer. He lived for a time in poverty among workers and down-and-outs in Paris and London, experiences described vividly in his first nonfiction book, Down and Out in London and Paris. Around 1933 he adopted the pen name George Orwell.
sections.title: Life

sections.content:
Orwell had already published novels such as Burmese Days, but his political awakening was sealed by the Spanish Civil War. In 1936 he married Eileen O’Shaughnessy. In late 1936 he left for Spain, where he fought on the Republican side. He was shot through the throat by a sniper and invalided out. The war convinced him both of the need to resist fascism and of the danger posed by Stalinist communism, which suppressed its own left-wing allies. His book Homage to Catalonia records those experiences with incomparable honesty, although it initially sold poorly.

During the Second World War, Orwell worked for the BBC and wrote some of his best-known essays, including essays on language and politics. He also began planning the two works for which he is now most remembered. Animal Farm is a political fable about a group of farm animals who overthrow their human master, only to be enslaved by their own pigs; it is a devastating critique of Stalinism and of the betrayal of revolutionary ideals. Nineteen Eighty-Four carried the same warning much further, imagining a technologically advanced totalitarian state where truth itself is a weapon. Completed as Orwell’s health was failing, it became his final book.
sections.title: Writing Career and Politics

sections.content: George Orwell died in London on 21 January 1950, aged 46, from tuberculosis. He survived just long enough to see at least some of the recognition his work would bring. In the decades since, his reputation has grown enormously. He is now regarded as one of the most influential British writers and political commentators of the twentieth century. Animal Farm and Nineteen Eighty-Four have sold tens of millions of copies and are read in schools around the world. Words such as Big Brother, Newspeak, doublethink, and Orwellian have become part of the global political vocabulary. Orwell’s commitment to plain language, honesty, and democratic socialism remains an enduring inspiration for writers and readers who believe that words should be used to speak truth to power.
